cards.title: Quadratic advantage of MA over AM proofs of proximity
cards.formal: Does there exist a family Π of finite-input properties admitting a Merlin–Arthur proof of proximity (MAP) of complexity O(√n) at every fixed positive proximity parameter, but for which every Arthur–Merlin proof of proximity (AMP) has complexity Ω(n) at some fixed positive proximity parameter ε₀? Here n is the full input-table length in bits and complexity is proof length plus input bits read. More precisely, ask for Π, a rational constant ε₀∈(0,1/2), and one MAP verifier V such that for every fixed rational ε∈(0,1) there are Cε,Nε with p_V(n)+q_V(n,ε)≤Cε√n for all admissible n≥Nε. For every AMP verifier W for Π there must be c_W>0,N_W such that p_W(n,ε₀)+q_W(n,ε₀)≥c_W n for every admissible n≥N_W. Neither bound hides factors growing with n. The same family and the same distance notion are used on both sides.
cards.why: Would determine whether keeping verifier randomness private achieves the largest possible advantage in minimally interactive verification of large inputs. The comparison isolates the information revealed to a prover while keeping proof length, input access and error requirements comparable.
cards.status_note: Read the 2018 source and the complete relevant definitions and open-question section in the journal version published 18 August 2021. Also checked ECCC TR18-083 revision 2, dated 9 May 2018. Subsequent-work searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of this unrestricted classical separation; quantum, sample-based and proof-oblivious results concern different models. Searches are not exhaustive.

cards.definitions:
To cover the source’s function properties, a candidate specifies an infinite decidable set I of admissible bit lengths, and, uniformly from n∈I, positive integers m(n),b(n) with m(n)b(n)=n and a finite alphabet Σ_n⊆{0,1}^{b(n)} of at least two symbols. An input is a table x∈Σ_n^{m(n)}, equivalently a function [m(n)]→Σ_n, and Π_n is a nonempty subset of these tables. The family and its finite alphabet descriptions must be mathematically specified; no polynomial-time membership test for Π is required. Boolean strings are the case b=1,m=n. Distance is Δ(x,Π_n)=min_{y∈Π_n}|{j:x_j≠y_j}|/m(n), the fraction of differing table entries, not the fraction of differing bits inside their symbols. A NO input has Δ>ε; members are YES inputs; no verdict is required for nonmembers with Δ≤ε. A query chooses j and reads x_j, charging b(n) bits. Queries may depend on the proof and on earlier answers. This is ordinary oracle access, not independent sampling, proof-oblivious access or a distribution-testing model. All n-asymptotics range over I.

A verifier is one finite, uniform oracle algorithm for the whole family, given n and rational ε∈(0,1) explicitly. It halts on every input, proof and random tape; it uses a finite computably bounded number of independent fair bits for each n,ε. Local computation and random bits are not charged and have no polynomial-time restriction. The prover knows the entire input and is computationally unrestricted. Proofs are binary strings of the specified length; shorter proofs may be padded, and oversized strings can be rejected without querying the input. Cost counts the whole permitted proof length, even if the verifier reads fewer proof bits. Query bounds hold for all inputs, proofs and randomness, not only in expectation.

For an MAP, the prover sends w before the verifier uses private randomness r. Completeness requires, for every n and x∈Π_n, a single w of length p(n), independent of ε and r, such that Pr_r[V^x(n,ε,w;r)=1]≥2/3 for every rational ε∈(0,1). Soundness requires Pr_r[V^x(n,ε,w;r)=1]≤1/3 for every allowed w when Δ(x,Π_n)>ε. For an AMP the verifier first reveals its entire random tape r, independently of the input; the prover then sends w=w(x,n,ε,r) of length p(n,ε). The verifier has no private or subsequently hidden coins and is deterministic given r. Completeness is Pr_r[∃w:W^x(n,ε,w;r)=1]≥2/3 for every member; soundness is Pr_r[∃w:W^x(n,ε,w;r)=1]≤1/3 for every ε-far input. Thus even a malicious prover may choose a different proof after each public tape. The public tape is not counted as communication in this model. Both protocols have exactly one prover message. No extra promise restricting the set of far tables is allowed. Constants in the MAP bound may depend on ε and the family; the AMP lower-bound constant may depend on W, but ε₀ is fixed once for the family.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer specifies one property family and proves both the MAP upper bound and the AMP lower bound in the stated model. A negative answer rules out such a family, for example through a sufficiently strong general simulation; failure of one candidate family is insufficient. A lower bound confined to nonadaptive or proof-oblivious AMP verifiers does not cover the required class. Polylogarithmic losses do not meet the exact O(√n) versus Ω(n) separation.

context_blocks.title: Why revealing coins can hurt
context_blocks.text: A private-coin verifier can choose tests after receiving a fixed proof. In an AMP the prover sees the entire tape and may tailor its answer to the verifier’s choices. The validity conditions therefore quantify over proofs in a different order even though only one prover message is sent.

context_blocks.title: The quadratic ceiling
context_blocks.text: The source gives a general conversion of an MAP with proof length p and query cost q to an AMP with the same proof length and query cost O((p+1)q). Thus an MAP of total cost c has an AMP of cost O(c²+c). Problem 6.2 asks whether a family can attain the corresponding square-root versus linear separation.

context_blocks.title: The proved separation goes the other way
context_blocks.text: The paper exhibits a permutation property with an AMP of O(log n) complexity at constant proximity and an MAP lower bound of Ω̃(n^{1/4}). This exponential advantage for AM does not answer the question of a quadratic advantage for MA. The separate results for proof-oblivious verifiers also do not resolve the unrestricted target.

context_blocks.title: Parameter convention
context_blocks.text: The open-problem display suppresses ε. This card states the constant-proximity reading explicitly: one MAP works for every fixed ε, with constants allowed to depend on ε, while the AMP lower bound already holds at one fixed ε₀. The input parameter counts all table bits, whereas distance counts changed table entries, as in the function model; variable alphabets are not treated as free one-bit answers.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
